summary: Describes a Virtual Private LAN Service built from pseudowires signaled with the Label Distribution Protocol. It creates an emulated LAN segment, a Layer 2 broadcast domain, for a group of users across a provider network.

plainLanguage.summary: VPLS lets customer sites in different places exchange Ethernet traffic as if they shared one LAN. Provider routers connect the sites with virtual wires and learn where each Ethernet address is located.

questions: how do pseudowires create a vpls
how does vpls learn mac addresses
subtitle: How provider routers use LDP-signaled pseudowires to join distant customer sites into one LAN.

tldr.problem: Customers at separate locations may need one Ethernet broadcast domain across a provider network.
tldr.mechanism: Provider Edge routers create a full mesh of pseudowires using LDP, learn MAC addresses from traffic, flood unknown destinations, and prevent loops with split horizon.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines a VPLS and a hierarchical option that reduces mesh size. RFC 4761 describes a similar service with different, incompatible signaling.

today: RFC 4762 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2007. Its IESG note says RFC 4761 provides a similar service using different, incompatible signaling.

sections.title: A LAN Service Across Multiple Sites
sections.content:
A Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) creates an emulated Layer 2 LAN for a set of customer sites. The service carries Ethernet frames across a provider network so the sites can share broadcast, multicast and unicast traffic.

The provider's interconnected Provider Edge (PE) devices form the service. Each PE connects customer equipment through an attachment circuit and sends frames to remote PEs over pseudowires. Several VPLS services can run on one PE.

The RFC's IESG note distinguishes this LDP-signaled method from RFC 4761. Both are called VPLS, but their signaling methods are incompatible.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS connects customer sites so their Ethernet devices can exchange frames across a provider network. The provider keeps each customer's LAN service separate.

sections.title: Full Mesh and Split Horizon
sections.content:
The basic VPLS topology is a full mesh: each PE has a pseudowire to every other PE in the service. With direct connections between every pair, a PE does not need to relay a frame from one pseudowire to another.

The RFC uses split horizon to prevent loops. A PE MUST NOT forward traffic received on one pseudowire to another pseudowire in the same VPLS mesh. Customer devices may still use spanning tree across their own redundant links.
sections.plainLanguage: Every provider-edge router connects directly to every other one in the same service. A router does not send a frame from one virtual wire onto another wire in that mesh.

sections.title: Flooding and Learning MAC Addresses
sections.content:
A PE floods broadcast, multicast and unknown-destination frames across the VPLS pseudowires and attachment circuits. It learns a source MAC address on the circuit or pseudowire where a frame arrives, then uses that association to forward later frames toward the address.

PEs SHOULD age out unused remote MAC entries. When a PE learns the same source address from a different pseudowire, it can update the association. The RFC also defines an optional LDP MAC List TLV to tell other PEs which addresses to forget after a topology change.
sections.plainLanguage: A PE remembers which connection sent a frame from a particular MAC address. If it does not know a destination, it sends the frame to all service connections.

sections.title: Signaling Pseudowires with LDP
sections.content:
PEs use a full mesh of LDP sessions to signal pseudowires. The Generalized PWid FEC Element identifies the VPLS and the pseudowire type. The VPLS MTU MUST match across every pseudowire in the mesh.

A MAC List TLV can accompany an LDP Address Withdraw message to remove learned addresses. Each address is six octets, so the TLV length must be a multiple of six. A PE that does not understand the optional withdrawal message can continue using the VPLS; stale entries age out or are replaced by later learning.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP lets the provider routers agree on the virtual wires for a VPLS. A withdrawal message can tell other routers to forget selected MAC addresses.

sections.title: Frames, VLANs and Learning Modes
sections.content:
A PE removes a customer-facing tag when that tag identifies the provider service, then restores a service tag when needed on exit. A VLAN tag that belongs to the customer's own network remains part of the frame.

Qualified learning, which MUST be supported, gives each customer VLAN its own VPLS instance and MAC address space. Optional unqualified learning puts all VLANs for one customer in one instance, so their MAC addresses must not overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider removes or adds only tags that identify its service. Customer VLAN tags stay with the customer's Ethernet frame.

sections.title: Hierarchical VPLS for Larger Networks
sections.content:
A full mesh requires n*(n-1)/2 pseudowires per VPLS. Hierarchical VPLS adds spoke connections from access devices to provider hubs, while the core provider routers retain their mesh. A bridging-capable access switch can use one spoke per service for multiple local connections.

A non-bridging PE can also connect through spokes, but it needs one pseudowire per attachment circuit. The RFC describes backup spokes and Ethernet access networks as additional ways to build larger services. In the Ethernet access model, a provider VLAN identifies a VPLS instance and the 4K instance limit applies within an Ethernet island.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of connecting every access device to every other device, a smaller access network can connect to provider hubs. This reduces the number of core connections needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says an unguarded VPLS can create risks for customers and providers. Separate per-VPLS forwarding tables and pseudowires isolate service traffic, but customer frames are carried unchanged.

If required, customers SHOULD encrypt or authenticate frames before they enter the provider network. The RFC also recommends LDP authentication and limits on the number of MAC addresses learned per site to reduce disruption and denial-of-service risk.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS separates each customer's forwarding information, but it does not encrypt customer frames. The RFC recommends protecting traffic and authenticating LDP messages where needed.

viz.caption: CORE RULES FOR A MESHED VPLS

items.title: Full mesh
items.text: Each PE has a pseudowire to every other PE in the VPLS.

items.title: Split horizon
items.text: A PE MUST NOT forward between pseudowires in the same mesh.

items.title: Learn from traffic
items.text: PEs associate source MAC addresses with the arriving connection.

items.title: Flood unknown traffic
items.text: Unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast frames are flooded.
